title: Problem Statement and Background
content:
**Erdős Problem #491** asks whether additive arithmetic functions with bounded consecutive differences must be essentially logarithmic. If f: ℕ → ℝ is additive (f(ab) = f(a) + f(b) when gcd(a,b) = 1) and |f(n+1) - f(n)| < c for all n, must f(n) = c'·log(n) + O(1)?

Erdős proved weaker versions in 1946 (vanishing differences or monotonicity force exact logarithmic behavior). Wirsing (1970) proved the full result under the weaker bounded-differences hypothesis.
mathContext: The result characterizes the logarithm among additive arithmetic functions. Additive functions are fundamental in analytic number theory, determined by their values on prime powers via the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.

title: Additive Function
content: **IsAdditive f** means f(1) = 0 and f(ab) = f(a) + f(b) whenever gcd(a,b) = 1. This is the standard definition in analytic number theory. Examples include the logarithm and the number-of-prime-factors function Ω(n). Unlike completely additive functions, additivity only requires the identity for coprime arguments.
mathContext: Additive functions are determined by their values on prime powers p^k. For completely additive functions, the values on primes alone suffice since f(p^k) = k·f(p).

title: Completely Additive and Its Relation to Additive
content:
**IsCompletelyAdditive f** strengthens additivity: f(ab) = f(a) + f(b) for ALL pairs a, b, not just coprime ones. The natural logarithm is the canonical example: log(ab) = log(a) + log(b) always.

**completely_additive_is_additive** proves the obvious implication: completely additive functions are additive (the coprimality hypothesis is simply dropped).
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of completely additive and its relation to additive

title: Bounded Consecutive Differences
content:
**HasBoundedDifferences f c** means c > 0 and |f(n+1) - f(n)| < c for all n ∈ ℕ. This is the key hypothesis in Erdős's problem — a regularity condition saying the function doesn't jump too much between consecutive integers.

**log_bounded_differences** axiomatizes that the logarithm satisfies this: log((n+1)/n) = log(1 + 1/n) ≤ log(2) for n ≥ 1.
mathContext: The bounded-differences condition is strictly weaker than requiring differences to tend to zero. Wirsing's result shows that even this weaker condition forces logarithmic behavior up to O(1).

title: Erdős's 1946 Results
content:
**erdos_1946_o1:** If f is additive and f(n+1) - f(n) → 0 (differences tend to zero), then f(n) = c·log(n) *exactly* for some constant c. No O(1) error term is needed.

**erdos_1946_monotone:** If f is additive and monotone (f(n+1) ≥ f(n)), then f(n) = c·log(n) with c ≥ 0. Monotonicity also forces exact logarithmic behavior.

Both results are stronger than Wirsing's theorem (exact rather than approximate), but require stronger hypotheses.
mathContext: These 1946 results motivated the 491 conjecture: if even bounded differences (not necessarily vanishing) suffice for an approximate characterization.

title: Wirsing's Theorem (1970)
content:
**IsLogPlusO1 f c'** means ∃ M > 0 such that |f(n) - c'·log(n)| ≤ M for all n ≥ 1. This captures 'f equals c'·log plus a bounded error.'

**wirsing_theorem:** The core result resolving Erdős #491. If f is additive with HasBoundedDifferences f c, then ∃ c' such that IsLogPlusO1 f c'. The O(1) error cannot be removed in general (unlike the vanishing-differences case).

**wirsingConstant** extracts the unique coefficient c' using Classical.choose.
mathContext: Wirsing's proof uses sophisticated techniques from analytic number theory, relating the behavior of f on consecutive integers to its values on prime powers through the structure of the integers.

title: Erdős Problem #491: Main Theorems
content:
**erdos_491** is the main entry point: additive + bounded differences implies f = c'·log + O(1). It is a direct application of wirsing_theorem.

**erdos_491_explicit** unpacks the existential to make the bound M explicit: ∃ c' M, M > 0 ∧ ∀ n ≥ 1, |f(n) - c'·log(n)| ≤ M.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of erdős problem #491: main theorems

title: Properties of the Characterization
content:
**wirsing_constant_unique:** The coefficient c' in f = c'·log + O(1) is unique. If f is within O(1) of both c'·log and c''·log, then c' = c''.

**wirsing_monotone_nonneg:** For monotone additive functions, c' ≥ 0 (the function grows like a non-negative multiple of log).

**log_unique_completely_additive:** For completely additive functions, the characterization sharpens to f = c'·log exactly (no O(1) error), since complete additivity provides enough structure to eliminate the bounded perturbation.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of properties of the characterization

title: Examples and Non-Examples
content:
**log_satisfies_hypothesis** (axiom): The logarithm itself satisfies bounded consecutive differences, confirming the hypothesis is non-vacuous.

**nonExample:** f(n) = n is a non-additive function with bounded differences (|1| < 2) that does NOT satisfy f = c·log + O(1), since n grows much faster than any c·log(n). This shows that the additivity hypothesis is essential — bounded differences alone don't force logarithmic behavior.

**non_example_bounded_diff** (theorem): Verified by norm_num that f(n) = n has HasBoundedDifferences with c = 2.
mathContext: See annotation content for formal details of examples and non-examples

title: Connection to Prime Factorization
content:
**additive_from_prime_powers:** An additive function f is determined by its values on prime powers: f(n) = Σ_{p | n} f(p^{v_p(n)}). This follows from the fundamental theorem of arithmetic and the additivity identity.

**additiveFromPrimes:** Constructs a completely additive function from any function g on primes by f(n) = Σ_{p | n} g(p)·v_p(n). This is the canonical construction showing that completely additive functions are determined by their values on primes alone.
mathContext: The prime factorization connection explains why additive functions are 'almost logarithmic': log(n) = Σ v_p(n)·log(p), which is exactly the additiveFromPrimes construction with g(p) = log(p).
